course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 1
unit.description: Follow Native American societies, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the Spanish empire from 1491 to 1607.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: European Exploration in the Americas
lesson.summary: Why Spain, Portugal, England, and France sent ships across the Atlantic: wealth, rivalry among monarchies, and the spread of Christianity.
learningGoals: Explain the economic, political, and religious causes of European exploration and conquest in the Americas.
Describe how navigation technology and royal sponsorship made long Atlantic voyages possible.
Explain how rivalry among European states shaped claims in the Americas.
lesson.bigIdea: European monarchies sought wealth, advantages over rivals, and religious expansion at the same time. Those motives overlapped, and together they explain why exploration became conquest.
lesson.context: The CED states one key concept for this topic: European efforts to explore and conquer the New World stemmed from a search for new sources of wealth, economic and military competition, and a desire to spread Christianity.

sections.title: Wealth, trade routes, and navigation

blocks.text: Spices, silk, and other Asian goods were valuable in Europe, and Italian merchants and Muslim intermediaries earned much of the profit. Rulers on the Atlantic edge of Europe wanted a share. Portugal sent ships down the African coast, and Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.

Spain's rulers, Ferdinand and Isabella, agreed in 1492 to fund Christopher Columbus's plan to reach Asia by sailing west. Columbus reached islands in the Caribbean instead. New ships and tools made such voyages possible. The caravel's triangular sails let it sail against the wind, and the magnetic compass and astrolabe helped sailors find direction and latitude.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Competition for trade with Asia led monarchs to pay for new routes, better ships made long voyages possible, and the voyages brought Europeans into contact with the Americas.

sections.takeaway: The search for wealth and trade routes, aided by new ships and navigation tools, sent Europeans across the Atlantic.

sections.title: Competition among European monarchies

blocks.text: Strong monarchies saw overseas wealth as a way to pay armies and gain power over rivals. Portugal and Spain moved first. Pope Alexander VI's 1493 decree and the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 drew a line that gave Spain most lands to the west and Portugal lands to the east, which later gave Portugal claim to Brazil.

Other states ignored these agreements. England sponsored John Cabot's voyage to North America in 1497, and France sent Giovanni da Verrazzano in 1524 and Jacques Cartier in 1534. Each state claimed land by right of discovery, and each hoped to keep rivals from gaining the same wealth.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The treaty divided claims between two Catholic states. It did not stop France or England from sending their own expeditions.

sections.takeaway: Rivalry pushed monarchies to claim territory quickly, and agreements between two states did not bind the others.

sections.title: Religion as a motive

blocks.text: Many Europeans saw conquest and conversion as linked. Spain had just completed the Reconquista, the centuries-long Christian campaign against Muslim rule in Iberia, and its rulers carried that crusading spirit across the ocean. Catholic monarchs sent priests with soldiers, and they argued that they had a duty to convert the peoples they met.

After the Protestant Reformation began in 1517, religion also sharpened rivalry. Protestant England and Catholic Spain became opponents, and promoters of colonies, such as Richard Hakluyt in his 1584 Discourse Concerning Western Planting, argued that English settlements could spread Protestant Christianity and weaken Spain. Wealth, rivalry, and faith were rarely separate motives.

sections.takeaway: Religious goals strengthened the economic and political reasons for exploration and gave conquest a moral justification.

connections.title: From voyages to exchange
connections.body: The voyages that these motives launched created the Columbian Exchange. Topic 1.4 explains what moved across the Atlantic and what happened to the societies that met.
connections.transferQuestion: Which motive for exploration, wealth, rivalry, or religion, do you think did most to turn exploration into conquest, and why?
connections.feedback: Take a position, give a specific example such as Spain after the Reconquista, and explain how your motive worked together with at least one other.
